A_target.statement:
Let $\mathbf A$ be an $n \times n$ [[Definition:Matrix|matrix]] over a [[Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)|field]] $K$ with $n$ distinct [[Definition:Eigenvalue of Matrix|eigenvalues]] in $K$.
Then $\mathbf A$ is [[Definition:Diagonalizable Matrix|diagonalizable]].

B_source.statement:
Let $\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_k$ be [[Definition:Eigenvector of Matrix|eigenvectors]] of $\mathbf A$ for pairwise distinct eigenvalues.
Then $\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_k$ are [[Definition:Linearly Independent Set|linearly independent]].

substitutions.the k independent eigenvectors: n eigenvectors, one for each eigenvalue

derived.an eigenbasis: a change of basis making A diagonal

object_map.reformulation: Reduce diagonalizability to the existence of a basis of eigenvectors.

validity_conditions: The eigenvalues must lie in K, so that the eigenvectors have entries in K.
n independent vectors in K^n form a basis.
proof_plan: Let $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$ be the distinct eigenvalues and choose eigenvectors $\mathbf v_i$ with $\mathbf A \mathbf v_i = \lambda_i \mathbf v_i$.
By the source result, $\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_n$ are linearly independent, hence a [[Definition:Basis (Linear Algebra)|basis]] of $K^n$.

Let $\mathbf P = \begin {bmatrix} \mathbf v_1 & \cdots & \mathbf v_n \end {bmatrix}$, which is invertible.
Then $\mathbf A \mathbf P = \mathbf P \mathbf D$ with $\mathbf D = \map {\operatorname {diag} } {\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n}$.

Hence $\mathbf P^{-1} \mathbf A \mathbf P = \mathbf D$, and $\mathbf A$ is diagonalizable.
{{qed}}
